newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan president vows to implement peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Sudan president vows to implement peace deal.

text.p: Sudan President Omar Hassan al-Bashir vowed to implement a peace deal signed on Monday with five former rebel factions which Khartoum hopes will help end a 14-year guerrilla war raging in the south.

But the opposition in exile said the deal was hollow because the factions which signed it did not include the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) of John Garang, the largest rebel group which has vowed to continue fighting the government.
But Bashir said Khartoum was resolved to end the war and "implement the accord...immediately and keep to its articles".
He declared an amnesty for members of groups signing the deal, which will be sent to parliament and public referendum.

Thousands of people turned out to attend the ceremony at the Khartoum palace. One guard was injured when the crowds broke down a door. After the ceremony, a display of firepower lit up the sky and doves were released to mark the occasion.
United States congressmen, a representative of South Africa, Central African Republic President Ange-Felix Patasse and Chad President Idriss Deby were among officials attending.

An official statement said the deal allows division of powers and wealth between federal and state governments, and says Islamic sharia is the main source of law but states may enact laws which complement it.

It says it prohibits discrimination, guarantees freedoms, and sees an interim period to rehabilitate the south, set up a democratic system and start a self-determination referendum in which southern citizens could choose unity or separation.

The opposition saw the deal as virtually meaningless because Garang's SPLA was not a party and said it was bound to fail because it was signed by government allies. They said it did not allow for a democratic, multi-party system.
"Such a regime based on fundamentalist ideals can never produce anything of a 'multi' nature," National Democratic Alliance (NDA) spokesman Farouq Abu Eissa told Reuters in Cairo.
The NDA is the umbrella opposition organisation which includes the SPLA and other rebel groups which since January have stepped up a campaign to topple the Islamist government.
Sudan has been riven by civil war since 1983, with the mainly Christian and animist south fighting what it sees as domination by the Moslem Arabised north.
Gabriel Mathiang, speaking in Cairo for the SPLA's political wing, said: "It is actually not going to work because they don't control the ground."

Former U.S. president Jimmy Carter, who met Bashir on Sunday, said in Addis Ababa on Monday that the Islamist government in Khartoum would have to forge peace with rebels and neighbours for Sudan's civil strife to end.
He said the peace deal that was signed on Monday has "some positive aspects".
Carter said however without the participation of the SPLA and the political opposition comprehensive peace in Sudan was unthinkable.
The groups which signed are splinter factions with few fighters, mostly fighting the SPLA as pro-government militias.
The deal finalises a 1996 charter Khartoum signed with SPLA -Bahr al-Ghazal and Southern Sudan Independence Movement.
Other factions later joined Khartoum's peace initiative and on Monday the Equatoria Defence Force, Independence Kawaz Makwei and Independence of Bor factions also signed the final accord.
A former opposition group, Union of Sudan African Parties, also signed the agreement and SPLA-Nuba signed separate deals.
